claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
Rapid solidification produces a fine, non-equilibrium matrix in the target alloy.
The target alloy has a relatively homogeneous elemental distribution before exposure.
High oxygen partial pressure selectively oxidizes Al, Cr, and Ti in the target alloy.
Oxidizing exposure forms a continuous, compositionally graded oxide scale.
The oxide scale formed at high oxygen partial pressure is protective and slows further degradation.
Reducing or low-oxygen conditions suppress robust oxide-scale formation.
Suppression of oxide-scale formation accelerates elemental segregation.
Enhanced elemental segregation under reducing conditions destabilizes the FCC matrix.
Destabilization of the FCC matrix produces brittle phases.
Brittle phases and local defects such as intergranular cracks coalesce into catastrophic failure.
Reactive-gas chemistry, represented primarily by oxygen partial pressure, governs high-temperature degradation.
Changing oxygen partial pressure changes the phase constitution or morphology of the resulting oxide scale.
Higher oxygen partial pressure produces a thicker oxide scale than lower oxygen partial pressure.
Oxidizing exposure produces a more homogeneous and adherent oxide scale.
Oxidizing exposure results in less internal segregation and less crack initiation than reducing exposure.
Reducing exposure produces a discontinuous or thinner oxide layer.
Reducing exposure produces greater segregation, earlier brittle-phase formation, and higher microcrack density.
The proposed governing behavior applies above 700°C for exposures of roughly 10–12 hours across oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
A lack of significant and reproducible changes in oxide morphology, segregation, or crack initiation when oxygen partial pressure is varied would falsify the proposed gas-chemistry mechanism.

contradictions.description: The design states that oxygen partial pressure is the only variable, but the proposed switch among O2-, H2-, and CO-containing gases also changes gas identity and chemical activity, introducing possible hydrogenation, carburization, and other atmosphere-specific effects.
